vignette:
Priya used to love the smell of metal and PVC cement. It was the smell of a job well done, of order restored from chaos. For twenty years, she’d been a plumber, the one people called when things went wrong. She took pride in her work, in the strength of her hands and the logical way her mind could trace a problem back to its source. Her husband, Sameer, would joke that she could diagnose a home’s entire plumbing system just by listening to it breathe. She used to believe him.

That changed eight months ago, on a Tuesday. It was a commercial kitchen renovation in an old downtown building. The air in the basement was already thick and damp, a familiar environment. While working to clear a blocked floor drain, a corroded feeder pipe from an adjacent chemical storage closet gave way. A thick, viscous liquid, later identified as a caustic solvent, flooded the small space. The smell hit her first—not like anything she’d ever encountered. It was sharp, acrid, and sweet all at once, an odor that didn’t just enter her nose but seemed to coat the inside of her lungs.

Her throat and eyes burned instantly. She began to cough, a deep, hacking cough that felt like it was tearing her apart from the inside. Disoriented and choking, she scrambled backward, slipping on the slick concrete and hitting her head. For a moment, the world was just the blinding smell, the burning in her chest, and the terrifying thought that she was breathing in poison, that she was going to die right there on a dirty basement floor. She managed to crawl to the stairs and haul herself into the main kitchen, gasping for air as the crew rushed to her side.

After a trip to the emergency room and a few days off work, the doctors assured her there was no permanent lung damage. But the event didn't end when her cough subsided. It replanted itself inside her.

Now, Priya’s world is a minefield of smells. The faint scent of bleach Sameer uses to clean the bathroom can send her reeling back to the basement, her heart hammering against her ribs as the phantom sensation of burning fills her throat. She’ll lock herself in the bedroom, towel stuffed under the door, until the smell is gone, leaving Sameer confused and hurt in the hallway. She threw out all her favorite scented candles and soaps. The cleaning aisle at the grocery store is a no-go zone; she’ll wait in the car while Sameer shops for the basics.

Work has become a source of dread. Every job site is a potential threat. Before she even unloads her tools, she stands in the doorway, sniffing the air like a frightened animal. Basements are the worst. The enclosed space, the damp air—it’s too close. She finds herself making excuses, turning down lucrative commercial jobs she would have jumped at a year ago, telling clients she’s “booked up.” Her confidence has evaporated. Her hands, once so steady, now sometimes tremble when she picks up a wrench. She feels like a fraud, a plumber who is terrified of pipes.

Sleep offers no escape. Most nights, she jolts awake from nightmares of drowning in that thick, sweet chemical, the smell so vivid she can taste it. She’ll lie in the dark for hours, her body rigid, listening to Sameer’s steady breathing and feeling utterly alone. She finds herself snapping at him over small things, then retreating into a wall of silence, ashamed of her own irritability. The easy laughter they once shared has become rare. She feels a profound distance from him, from everyone. She sees the worry in his eyes but doesn’t know how to explain that the problem isn’t in her lungs anymore; it’s taken root in her mind, and she, the woman who could diagnose a hidden leak by sound alone, has no idea how to fix it.
